q: A table has 8 indexes. What does that do to an INSERT?
options: The row is written into the table and into all 8 indexes, so the INSERT is slower
Only the primary key index is written
The INSERT is faster, because the data is sorted
why: Every index is written on every INSERT. More indexes, slower writes.

q: What happens when a B-tree page is full and a new key must go in?
options: The tree is rebuilt from scratch
why: Keys that arrive in order split only on the right edge, which is cheap.

q: An UPDATE changes one non-indexed column, but it is not a HOT update. What does it write?
options: Only an entry in the primary key index
A new entry in every index of the table, even for columns you did not change
A new copy of every index
why: The new row version has a new address, so every index must learn it.

q: What does a HOT update need?
options: A unique index on the changed column
No indexed column changed, and room on the same page. A lower fillfactor leaves room

q: Postgres ignores your index for `WHERE country = 'US'` when most rows are US. Why is that fine?
options: When most rows match, reading the table once is cheaper than jumping through the index
why: An index helps when few rows match.

q: Which index kind suits a huge table whose rows arrive in the order of one column, like a timestamp?
why: Default to B-tree. Think BRIN for huge tables that grow in the order of one column.

q: How can you find indexes nobody uses?
options: Look at the index file size
Count the columns in the index
Check `idx_scan` in the statistics. An index with zero scans costs on every write for no reason
why: Check idx_scan over a long enough time, then drop with care.
